lead: Quality factor Q measures how much energy a resonant circuit stores compared with what it loses each cycle. It is a single number that sets two practical properties: bandwidth and selectivity. High Q gives a narrow bandwidth, so the circuit responds strongly only near its resonant frequency and rejects nearby frequencies. Low Q gives a broad, gentle response. This idea is used in radio tuning, filters, wireless receivers and any circuit where one frequency must be picked out from many. This chapter defines Q from energy, connects it to bandwidth and selectivity, and gives the series and parallel formulas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 and Chapter 4.2 for series and parallel resonance, and Unit 3 for AC power and the half-power idea.

blocks.text: At resonance, a series RLC circuit stores energy in the inductor's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field. The current and voltage oscillate at f₀, while the energy stored in L and C oscillates and is exchanged at 2f₀. In the ideal lossless case the total stored energy is constant. The resistor removes energy as heat every cycle. Q compares the energy kept to the energy lost.

blocks.where: W<sub>stored,peak</sub> is the peak energy stored in L or C in joules (J); W<sub>lost,cycle</sub> is the energy lost in R per cycle in joules (J); Q is dimensionless.

blocks.text: For a series RLC at resonance, W<sub>stored,peak</sub> = ½ L I₀² and the energy lost per cycle is (I₀²/2) R T, where I₀ is peak current in amperes (A), T = 1/f₀ is the period in seconds (s), L is inductance in henries (H), C is capacitance in farads (F), and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). Substituting into the energy definition gives the series result.

blocks.where: ω₀ = 2πf₀ is the resonant angular frequency in rad/s; f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) is the resonant frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: For a parallel RLC near resonance, the same energy definition gives a reciprocal use of R. The shunt resistor removes less energy when R is large, so Q rises with R.

blocks.where: R is the shunt resistance in ohms (Ω); L and C are the same as above.

blocks.text: A larger series R lowers Q and widens the response. A larger parallel R raises Q and narrows the response. Check which circuit you have before substituting R.

Bandwidth BW is the frequency range between the two half-power frequencies f₁ and f₂. At these frequencies the power in R is half its maximum. In a series circuit the current magnitude is I₀/√2 ≈ 0.707I₀; in a parallel circuit the voltage magnitude is V₀/√2, where V₀ is the peak voltage across the parallel RLC circuit at resonance. The half-power points are also called the −3 dB points.

blocks.where: f₁ is the lower half-power frequency in Hz; f₂ is the upper half-power frequency in Hz; BW is in Hz.

blocks.text: At resonance a series RLC has impedance R. At a half-power point the impedance magnitude is |Z| = √(R² + (ωL − 1/(ωC))²) = R√2. Solving this condition gives the exact half-power angular frequencies.

blocks.where: ω₁ is the lower half-power angular frequency; ω₂ is the upper half-power angular frequency; Q is the resonant quality factor.

blocks.text: The exact half-power frequencies are not exactly evenly spaced around f₀; they are symmetric about f₀√(1 + 1/(4Q²)). For Q ≥ 10 that factor is almost 1, so the half-power frequencies are close to f₀ and approximately evenly spaced.
f₁ ≈ f₀ − BW/2,  f₂ ≈ f₀ + BW/2
blocks.where: f₀ is the resonant frequency in Hz; BW is the bandwidth in Hz; the approximation is valid for Q ≥ 10.

blocks.text: The bandwidth follows directly from Q. In angular units the bandwidth is ω<sub>BW</sub> = ω₂ − ω₁. For a series RLC, ω<sub>BW</sub> = R/L exactly; for a parallel RLC, ω<sub>BW</sub> = 1/(RC) exactly.
BW = f₀ / Q,   ω<sub>BW</sub> = ω₀ / Q
blocks.where: f₀ and BW are in Hz; ω₀ and ω<sub>BW</sub> are in rad/s; Q is dimensionless.

blocks.text: Selectivity is how well a circuit picks the wanted frequency and rejects nearby unwanted frequencies. It is measured by the selectivity ratio BW/f₀ = 1/Q. A small ratio means a sharp peak and good selectivity; a large ratio means a broad response and poor selectivity.
Two radio stations 10 kHz apart can be separated by a filter with BW = 5 kHz. A filter with BW = 50 kHz passes both and cannot separate them. The narrower filter has the higher Q.

High Q gives narrow bandwidth and high selectivity. Low Q gives wide bandwidth and low selectivity. Very high Q also makes the tuned frequency sensitive to component tolerance, temperature and loading, so receivers often use moderate Q with careful tuning.

For a series RLC the damping ratio is ζ = 1/(2Q). A high-Q circuit has small ζ and rings for many cycles after a disturbance. The transient meaning of ζ belongs to Unit 5; here the link only shows how Q controls damping.

figure.caption: Current response versus normalized frequency for Q = 5, 20 and 50. The Q = 50 curve has the narrowest peak, so it has the smallest bandwidth and the sharpest selectivity.

spec.aria: Selectivity curves for Q = 5, 20 and 50; higher Q gives a narrower peak and a smaller bandwidth around f₀.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has a resonant frequency f₀ = 1 kHz and a quality factor Q = 50. Find the bandwidth, the two half-power frequencies, and the selectivity ratio. Use the high-Q approximation.
steps: Write the given values: f₀ = 1 kHz = 1000 Hz, Q = 50. The approximation is allowed because Q ≥ 10.
Lower half-power frequency: f₁ ≈ f₀ − BW/2 = 1000 − 10 = 990 Hz.
Upper half-power frequency: f₂ ≈ f₀ + BW/2 = 1000 + 10 = 1010 Hz.
examples.answer: The bandwidth is 20 Hz, the half-power frequencies are about 990 Hz and 1010 Hz, and the selectivity ratio is 0.02 (2%).
examples.check:
f0 = 1000.0
Q = 50.0
BW = f0 / Q
f1 = f0 - BW / 2
f2 = f0 + BW / 2
ratio = BW / f0
print(BW)
print(f1)
print(f2)
print(ratio)

traps: Inverse relation: Higher Q means smaller BW, not larger. If BW falls by a factor of 2, Q rises by a factor of 2 at the same f₀.
Unit mix-up: BW = f₀/Q gives hertz only when f₀ is in hertz. ω<sub>BW</sub> = ω₀/Q gives rad/s. Multiplying or dividing by 2π at the wrong step changes the answer.
Series and parallel R: Q<sub>series</sub> = ω₀L/R falls as R rises, while Q<sub>parallel</sub> = R/(ω₀L) rises as R rises. Using the wrong formula reverses the effect of R.
Approximation limit: f₁,₂ = f₀ ± BW/2 is only good for Q ≥ 10. For low Q the exact half-power frequencies are not evenly spaced around f₀.
Selectivity ratio confusion: BW/f₀ = 1/Q is a fraction; 0.02 is 2%, not 0.02%. Also do not call the ratio a bandwidth.

quiz.q: Define the quality factor Q of a resonant circuit from energy.
quiz.a: Q = 2π × (peak energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle). It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does a higher Q give a narrower bandwidth?
quiz.a: Q = f₀/BW, so for a fixed f₀ a larger Q means a smaller BW. The circuit loses a smaller fraction of its stored energy per cycle, so its response falls off faster away from resonance.

quiz.q: A series RLC circuit has f₀ = 2 kHz and Q = 40. Find BW and the approximate half-power frequencies.
quiz.a: BW = 2000/40 = 50 Hz. BW/2 = 25 Hz, so f₁ ≈ 1975 Hz and f₂ ≈ 2025 Hz. Q ≥ 10 so the approximation is valid.

quiz.q: Two series RLC circuits have the same f₀ = 100 kHz. Circuit A has Q = 10 and circuit B has Q = 50. Compare their bandwidths and selectivity. Which separates two stations 2 kHz apart better?
quiz.a: BW_A = 100000/10 = 10 kHz; BW_B = 100000/50 = 2 kHz. B has one-fifth the bandwidth and selectivity ratio 1/50 = 0.02 versus 0.1 for A. B is much sharper, so it separates the two stations 2 kHz apart better.

quiz.q: What is meant by a half-power frequency? What is the voltage or current ratio there?
quiz.a: It is a frequency where the power in the resistance is half the maximum power. The current or voltage magnitude is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 of its maximum value.

quiz.q: A parallel RLC has f₀ = 50 kHz and BW = 500 Hz. Find Q and the selectivity ratio.
A series RLC has Q = 8 and f₀ = 10 kHz. Can you use f₁,₂ = f₀ ± BW/2? Explain and state what to do instead.
quiz.a: No. Q = 8 is below the stated Q ≥ 10 limit, so do not rely on the approximation. BW = 10000/8 = 1250 Hz. Compute f₁ and f₂ from the exact expression or from |Z| = R√2.

beyond: Not for the exam. In RF design, loaded Q and unloaded Q decide whether a filter can reject a strong nearby transmitter without killing the wanted weak signal. Crystal and SAW filters reach very high Q because their resonators lose little energy per cycle. On-chip inductors have low Q, so radio chips often use active filters or external components.
